strengths: Comprehensive unified framework successfully integrating 9 diverse motion-related tasks (synthesis and comprehension) through a single model—addressing an important gap in the field

Novel MotionHub dataset with 70+ hours of multimodal motion data (131,512 single-person and 62,791 dual-person descriptions) represents a substantial community contribution with strong scale and diversity

Well-designed HoMi Tokenizer combining VQ-VAE with Frequency-Aware Motion Gating for effective holistic motion encoding; pragmatic design using separate torso/hand encoders while maintaining body coherence

Extensive experimental validation across 9 tasks with task-specific evaluation metrics; achieves competitive or state-of-the-art performance on multiple tasks (T2M, M2T, music-to-dance, dual-person text-to-motion)
Thorough ablation studies examining codebook size (Table 12), tokenizer components (Table 9), and motion representations (Table 11); demonstrates systematic experimental methodology
Clear presentation with effective architectural diagrams and comprehensive result tables; good visualization of generated outputs across diverse tasks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: HoMi Tokenizer primarily combines existing VQ-VAE/RVQ techniques; frequency-aware gating lacks theoretical justification and shows marginal improvements (Table 9). LLaMA-3 fine-tuning is straightforward transfer learning

Unclear multi-task training strategy: paper lacks details on task weighting, gradient balancing, and sampling across 9 tasks. No ablation isolating single-task vs. multi-task benefits or evidence that unified training improves performance relative to task-specific models

Insufficient dataset documentation: motion capture protocols, annotation procedures, and quality control measures not clearly described. Extent of manual annotation for audio-motion alignment unclear. No discussion of dataset biases or inter-annotator agreement

Incomplete experimental analysis: missing recent baselines for some tasks (especially M2D), absent human evaluation studies despite relying heavily on automatic metrics (FID, R-Precision), no systematic failure analysis or discussion of when unified approach underperforms

Unaddressed motion representation limitations: paper acknowledges (Appendix C.1.2) that global joint coordinates accumulate errors in multi-person settings but provides no solution. Trade-offs between coordinate systems inadequately analyzed despite visible impact on reconstruction quality (Table 11)

Reproducibility and technical clarity concerns: codebook size selection lacks principled justification; LLaMA-3 configuration sparse; no variance reporting across random seeds; critical training details (task sampling, convergence) missing

Limited evidence of unified framework advantages: Table 2 shows unified model sometimes underperforms task-specific T2M baselines. Paper doesn't clearly articulate when/why unified approach should be preferred over task-specific models for practitioners
No computational efficiency analysis: inference latency, memory requirements, and scalability to longer sequences not discussed. Practical feasibility for real-world deployment unclear

Scattered scope with uneven treatment: attempting to cover 9 tasks; some (Speech-to-Gesture, Reconstruction Quality Evaluation) underdeveloped. Dense presentation with important methodological details relegated to appendix

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 9 diverse motion-related tasks demonstrates broad applicability and achieves competitive or state-of-the-art results
MotionHub dataset aggregates 70.10 hours of multimodal motion data (131,515 single-person and 62,791 dual-person sequences), providing a useful resource for the community
Practical technical contribution: frequency-aware motion gating in the HoMi Tokenizer is a sensible design choice addressing quantization loss in the frequency domain
Implementation details provided with promise of code/data release supports reproducibility and community adoption
Strong quantitative results across multiple benchmarks (Tables 2-8) with improvements in R-Precision, FID, and other metrics
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: HoMi Tokenizer is an incremental modification of VQ-VAE; multimodal motion LLMs (MotionGPT, M²GPT) already combine LLMs with motion; core contribution reduces to engineering existing methods
Overstated 'unified framework' claim: The approach performs standard multi-task instruction-tuning with task-specific prompts, not fundamentally different from generic multi-task LLM fine-tuning

Critical ablation studies missing: No comparison of HoMi vs. vanilla VQ-VAE performance, no analysis of unified vs. task-specific training benefits, no component-wise ablation—these are essential to justify design claims

Unclear experimental fairness: Insufficient detail on whether baseline comparisons use identical training data; improvements are sometimes modest (2-3% relative gains without statistical significance testing)
Insufficient analysis of results: Limited insight into why the method works; no error analysis, failure case discussion, or investigation of which tasks benefit from multimodal pretraining

MotionHub contribution overstated: The dataset is primarily a curation of existing datasets (AIST++, FineDance, BEAT) rather than novel captures; claim of 'most extensive multitask dataset' insufficiently justified
Presentation clarity issues: Main contribution remains unclear (tokenizer? framework? dataset? results?); dense paper covering 9 tasks lacks depth; Figure 2 is complex and hard to parse
Missing depth in technical contribution: Training strategy is straightforward pretraining + instruction-tuning without novel learning objectives or theoretical insights
Insufficient documentation of prompt design and training procedures for reproducibility; unclear how 'unified' training differs operationally from separate task-specific fine-tuning
Evaluation metrics inconsistency across tasks; some metrics (e.g., specific FID definitions) are non-standard; lack of unified performance assessment

strengths: Comprehensive unified framework effectively addressing both motion synthesis and comprehension across 9 diverse tasks with extensive empirical validation
Well-designed HoMi Tokenizer with frequency-aware motion gating using FFT and separate torso/hand encoding demonstrates careful technical engineering
Large-scale MotionHub dataset with 70.10 hours of motion data, careful data integration, and unified coordinate system provides valuable resource for community
Strong and consistent empirical results across multiple tasks with proper evaluation metrics (R-Precision, BLEU, FID, MMD, etc.) and thorough ablation studies (Tables 9, 11)
Two-stage training strategy (pretraining + instruction tuning) is well-motivated with clear implementation details supporting reproducibility; code and data promised publicly
Excellent presentation quality with clear figures explaining pipeline, architecture, and results; logical paper structure facilitating understanding
weaknesses: Limited individual algorithmic novelty: HoMi Tokenizer builds directly on VQ-VAE with FFT gating; LLaMA-3 uses standard fine-tuning without architectural innovations; main contribution is component integration rather than fundamental breakthroughs
Evaluation restricted to single dataset (MotionHub): no cross-dataset generalization studies, zero-shot evaluation, or testing on independent motion datasets limits generalization claims

Some performance improvements over baselines are modest and lack statistical significance testing (e.g., Table 2 M2T: marginal differences; Table 3 shows comparable performance to single-task methods)

Dataset contribution primarily organizational consolidation of existing sources (AIST++, FineDance, HumanML3D) rather than novel motion capture or annotation methodology; limited dataset-specific innovation

Insufficient multi-task learning analysis: no investigation of task interference, which task combinations benefit joint training, or negative transfer; missing ablation isolating impact of unified training vs. single-task variants

Design choice justification gaps: separate torso/hand encoding shows only modest improvements (Table 9); FFT-based gating lacks theoretical motivation; codebook size sensitivity (Table 12) suggests hyperparameter brittleness with minimal discussion

Absent failure analysis: no discussion of error types, challenging motion categories, performance on rare actions, or behavior on non-standard motion types; generalization to out-of-distribution motions unexplored

Methodological concerns: no statistical confidence intervals; instruction tuning design not deeply justified; LoRA parameters unexplored through ablation; Figure 4 shows significant codebook utilization drop without efficiency implications discussed
